title: How to tell how far away lightning is (count, then divide)
description:
Light crosses a kilometre in about 3 millionths of a second; sound, at 343 metres a second, needs about 3 seconds (5 seconds per mile). So count the seconds from flash to thunder and divide by 3 for kilometres: 15 seconds is 5 km. The rumble is the whole bolt arriving piece by piece: if its near end is 2 km away and its far end 5 km, you hear it from 6 to 15 seconds. Count again two minutes later: 12 seconds means 4 km, so the storm closes 1 km every 2 minutes and reaches you in about 8.

Numbers checked in code: light and sound travel times, the example counts, and 200,000 simulated strikes 1 to 15 km away at 0 to 30 C with counts rounded to the second (the divide-by-3 rule lands within about half a kilometre 95% of the time). Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thunder, Environment and Climate Change Canada "How thunder sounds".

beats.say: Flash: 3 millionths of a second. Thunder: 3 seconds.
Same kilometre. You don't need a weather radar. That gap is a ruler.
Light covers 300,000 kilometres a second. Sound only does 343 metres.
Step 1: lightning flashes. Count the seconds until the thunder. Say you get to 15.
Step 2: divide by 3. The strike was 5 kilometres away. For miles, divide by 5.
Why does it rumble? The bolt is kilometres long. Its near end is 2 away, its far end 5. You hear the near end at 6 seconds and the far end at 15.
That tells you where it is. Now find out when it gets here.
Step 3: count again two minutes later. 12 seconds. That's 4 kilometres, so it moved 1 kilometre in 2 minutes.
4 kilometres left, at 1 every 2 minutes: it's overhead in about 8.
Two counts and one division, and you know where the storm is and when it arrives.
So the next flash, you count to 21. How far away was it?
